findings.title: Validation has a side effect that inflates blocked-email match counts
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and last_match_at and saves the row. Validations are not idempotent reads: User#valid? is called explicitly in UsersController#create (`if user.valid? && SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub?`) and again inside user.save, and change_username also calls valid?. A single signup attempt therefore counts as two or more matches, so match_count and last_match_at stop meaning how often the address tried to register. Any caller that validates a User for another reason (for example a console check or a background job) also increments the counter. The check should be a pure lookup, with the statistics recorded only when a registration is actually rejected.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count
findings.body: should_block? loads the record, does `record.match_count += 1` in Ruby and then calls save. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked address both read the same count and both write count+1, so increments are lost. An atomic SQL update (`BlockedEmail.where(id: ...).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')`) would avoid this. Calling record.save also runs the model's validations on every match and can silently fail, leaving the counter unchanged.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive while users' emails are not normalized
findings.body: should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` with the raw value, and nothing downcases the address on the way in. User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] directly, so 'Bad@SpamClub.com' will not match a blocklist entry for 'bad@spamclub.com'. The blocklist is trivially bypassed by changing the case of the address. The code elsewhere uses Email.downcase for emails, so the lookup should normalize the same way, and the stored entries should be normalized too.

findings.title: Response reveals that an email is on the blocklist
findings.body: The create failure response now includes errors.to_hash, and the blocked case adds the message 'is not allowed.' under the email key. Anyone can POST to /users with a candidate address and learn whether it is blocklist-listed, and each probe also increments match_count. This is an enumeration oracle for the blocklist. The response should give a generic message for blocked addresses, or the blocklist error should be kept out of the client-visible errors.

findings.title: Whitelist and blacklist behavior moved into the validator without tests
findings.body: The domain whitelist and blacklist logic was moved out of User into EmailValidator in this change, but the spec only covers the BlockedEmail path with stubbed should_block?. Nothing checks that email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist still reject addresses, or that the not_allowed message is still added. The blocked-email check also runs only when no earlier error exists, which is untested. There is also no test that validation does not increment match_count for a valid address or a repeated validation.

findings.title: Unique index on a non-normalized email column
findings.body: The unique index is on the raw email string, so 'Bad@x.org' and 'bad@x.org' can both be inserted as separate blocklist entries. Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in should_block?, duplicate and inconsistent entries are possible. Normalizing the email before save, or indexing on a lowercased value, would prevent this.

findings.title: Rejected emails stay blocked for the whole controller lifetime
findings.body: rejectedEmails is an array on a singleton controller, and every address pushed by the failure callback is treated as invalid until the page reloads. Any server rejection for an email, including transient or unrelated errors such as a uniqueness or hub error, permanently marks that address invalid in the client. The client also never clears this list, and the only way to recover is to change the address. Since the server already reports the field error, the client should rely on the server response rather than keep its own permanent blocklist.
